Description: explicit — client-side hypsometric tint (color-relief layer, GL JS 5.6+)
prompt: I have terrain tiles as a raster-dem source in MapLibre GL JS and I want to color the map by elevation ranges (a hypsometric tint) directly client-side — blues at sea level through greens and browns to white peaks — without pre-rendering colored raster tiles. What layer type do I use and how do I configure the color ramp?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer** *Use a **`color-relief`** layer.* It reads the same `raster-dem` source you already have and lets you paint the DEM directly with an **`["elevation"]`** expression. The colour ramp is defined in the `color-relief-color` paint property with an `interpolate` expression. --- ## 1. Add (or keep) the DEM source ```js // You probably already have this – it must be a raster-dem source map.addSource('terrain-dem', { type: 'raster-dem', url: 'https://my.tileserver.com/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.webp', // any DEM format you use // optional: encoding: 'terrarium' | 'mapbox' | 'raw' … maxzoom: 12 }); ``` > **Note** – The source stays a `raster-dem`. Nothing changes for the colour-relief layer; it just points at the same source. --- ## 2. Add a `color-relief` layer ```js map.addLayer({ id: 'hypsometric-tint', type: 'color-relief', // ← the layer type that does the job source: 'terrain-dem', paint: { // 1️⃣ The colour ramp – an interpolate over the special ["elevation"] expression 'color-relief-color': [ 'interpolate', ['linear'], // linear interpolation between stops ['elevation'], // elevation in metres (relative to the DEM's datum) // ── Elevation (m) ── ── Colour ─────────────────────────────────────── 0, '#2c7bb6', // deep ocean – dark blue 50, '#3b8cc4', // shallow water – lighter blue 200, '#5fa5d0', // near-shore – cyan-ish 500, '#8cc0a1', // lowland – teal/green 1000, '#b8e186', // foothills – light green 1500, '#e6f598', // mid-elevation – yellow-green 2000, '#fee08b', // sub-alpine – pale yellow 2500, '#fdbb84', // alpine – orange-brown 3000, '#fc8d59', // high alpine – orange-red 3500, '#e34a33', // rock – reddish brown 4000, '#b30000', // bare rock / snow line – dark red 4500, '#ffffff' // peaks – pure white ], // 2️⃣ Optional opacity (default = 1) 'color-relief-opacity': 0.85, // 3️⃣ Optional resampling mode (GL JS 5.20+) // 'resampling': 'linear' // or 'nearest' } }); ``` ### What the snippet does | Part | Why it matters | |------|----------------| | `type: 'color-relief'` | The only layer type that can colour a DEM client-side. | | `['elevation']` | A **special expression** that returns the elevation (in metres) of the pixel currently being rendered. It can **only** be used inside `color-relief-color`. | | `interpolate` | Generates a smooth gradient between the stops you define. Use `linear` (or `exponential` if you want a non-linear ramp). | | Elevation stops | Choose the heights that match your colour palette. The example goes from sea-level blue → green → brown → white, but you can add, remove or reorder stops as you like. | | `color-relief-opacity` | Controls overall transparency; useful if you want to see an underlying imagery layer. | | `resampling` (optional) | Determines how the DEM is sampled when the map is zoomed. `linear` gives smoother colour transitions; `nearest` is a bit sharper and a little faster. | --- ## 3. Full minimal example (HTML + JS) ```html MapLibre – Hypsometric colour-relief
``` Open the page, pan/zoom, and you’ll see the DEM coloured directly in the browser – no pre-rendered coloured tiles required. --- ## 4. Common pitfalls & how to avoid them | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | The layer shows **grey/black** instead of colours | You used a `raster` layer or `raster-color` property (Mapbox-only) | Switch to `type: 'color-relief'` and use `color-relief-color`. | | The ramp looks **flat** (all one colour) | The expression is not inside `color-relief-color` or you used `["elevation"]` in a different layer type | `["elevation"]` works **only** inside `color-relief-color`. | | Colours are **wrongly shifted** (e.g., sea-level appears brown) | The DEM’s **encoding** (terrarium, mapbox, raw) does not match the source definition, so the elevation values are mis-interpreted. | Set the correct `encoding` property on the `raster-dem` source (`encoding: 'terrarium'` etc.). | | Performance drops when zoomed in | Very dense DEM tiles + a huge number of stops can be heavy on low-end devices. | Keep the ramp to a reasonable number of stops (10-15) and use `color-relief-opacity` < 1 if you also have a low-resolution base map underneath. | | Nothing shows up after adding the layer | The source URL is wrong, or the source isn’t loaded before the layer is added. | Add the layer **after** the `load` event (or after `source` `data` event). | --- ## 5. TL;DR cheat-sheet ```json { "id": "hypsometric-tint", "type": "color-relief", "source": "terrain-dem", "paint": { "color-relief-color": [ "interpolate", ["linear"], ["elevation"], 0, "#2c7bb6", 200, "#8cc0a1", 1000, "#b8e186", 2000, "#fee08b", 3000, "#fc8d59", 4000, "#b30000", 4500, "#ffffff" ], "color-relief-opacity": 0.9 } } ``` *That’s it – a hypsometric tint drawn entirely on the client, powered by the `color-relief` layer.*

Description: anti-pattern — stacking hillshade layers for multi-directional shading
prompt: My single hillshade layer in MapLibre GL JS looks harsh, how do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Why a Hillshade Can Look “Harsh” A **single** `hillshade` layer is already enough to give you relief. If the result is: * very black shadows / very white highlights * “chalky” ridges that dominate the underlying map * a flat-looking surface that only shows a stark black-and-white relief the problem is almost always one (or a combination) of these paint settings: | Property | What it does | Typical harsh default | |----------|--------------|-----------------------| | `hillshade-method` | How the light is computed. `standard` (default) uses a single light source. | Single-direction lighting → strong, high-contrast shadows | | `hillshade-exaggeration` | Scales the slope before shading. | Values > 0.5 make slopes look too steep | | `hillshade-illumination-direction` | Azimuth of the light (0-360°). | A direction that points straight from the top of the screen can make shadows fall straight onto the map, looking “flat-black”. | | `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | Whether the light follows the viewport (`viewport`) or the map (`map`). | `viewport` keeps the light fixed to the screen, so when you rotate the map the shadows don’t rotate – they can look unnatural. | | `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` | Colours of the dark and bright parts. | Opaque black / white → harsh contrast. | --- ## Quick Fixes (no extra layers needed) ### 1. Use the **multidirectional** method (GL JS ≥ 5.5) `multidirectional` lights the terrain from several independent directions in **one pass**. It gives a softer, more natural look and removes the need to stack several hillshade layers. ```json { "id": "hillshade", "type": "hillshade", "source": "terrain-dem", "paint": { "hillshade-method": "multidirectional", "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.4, // a little less than the default 0.5 "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map", // light rotates with the map "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)", // cool, semi-transparent shadows "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)" // warm, semi-transparent highlights } } ``` **Why it works** * **One layer, one draw pass** – no performance penalty. * The combined light directions smooth out the black-white extremes. * Adding a little transparency to the shadow/highlight colours lets the underlying imagery show through, further softening the effect. ### 2. Tweak the other paint properties (optional) If you still need a bit more control, adjust any of the following: ```json { "paint": { "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35, // lower → flatter shading "hillshade-illumination-direction": 315, // change the main light azimuth "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map", // keep light fixed to map orientation "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(20,30,60,0.35)", "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,250,220,0.3)" } } ``` * **Exaggeration**: values between 0.2 – 0.5 are usually pleasant. * **Direction**: try 315° (north-west) or 45° (north-east) to see which matches your data best. * **Anchor**: `map` makes the light rotate with the map, which often looks more natural when the user pans/rotates. ### 3. **Never stack multiple hillshade layers** to get a softer look Before GL JS 5.5 the only way to approximate multidirectional lighting was to add several `hillshade` layers with different `hillshade-illumination-direction`s. That required extra draw passes and still produced harsher results. Now you can achieve the same (and better) effect with the single `hillshade-method: "multidirectional"` property. --- ## Full Minimal Example ```html Soft Hillshade with MapLibre GL JS
``` *Replace the DEM URL with the one you are already using.* The map will render the satellite imagery draped over a softly shaded terrain surface. --- ## Checklist – Did you address the common “harsh hillshade” symptoms? | ✅ | Check | |----|-------| | **Single hillshade layer** (no stacked copies) | | `hillshade-method` set to **`multidirectional`** (GL JS ≥ 5.5) | | `hillshade-exaggeration` ≤ 0.5 (usually 0.3-0.4) | | Shadow & highlight colours have **alpha** (e.g., `rgba(...,0.4)`) | | `hillshade-illumination-anchor` set to **`map`** (optional but often improves realism) | | If you still see harshness, tweak `hillshade-illumination-direction` or the colour alphas a bit more. | --- ### TL;DR 1. **Set** `"hillshade-method": "multidirectional"` – one layer, one pass, soft lighting. 2. **Lower** `"hillshade-exaggeration"` to ~0.4 (or less). 3. **Add transparency** to `"hillshade-shadow-color"` and `"hillshade-highlight-color"` (e.g., `rgba(...,0.4)`). 4. **Optional:** change `"hillshade-illumination-anchor"` to `"map"` and adjust the direction if you want a specific sun angle. 5. **Never** stack multiple hillshade layers – the single-layer multidirectional method replaces that old hack. That’s all you need to turn a harsh, black-and-white hillshade into a smooth, natural-looking relief surface. Happy mapping!
